subChunks.title: Votes, Trades & the Paper Trail of Work
subChunks.hookHtml: Between census years, families are nearly invisible in official records. Electoral registers, trade directories, rate books, and occupational records — guild memberships, apprenticeship records, professional licensing — fill that silence. They track addresses year by year, reveal social mobility through changing occupations, and sometimes provide the single piece of evidence that connects a known name to a specific location at a specific time.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Electoral registers (UK)

From 1832, British electoral registers listed every man who qualified to vote in parliamentary elections. The qualification thresholds changed several times — the Reform Act 1832 introduced a property qualification; the 1867 Act extended the vote to many working-class men; universal male suffrage came in 1918; women over 30 got the vote in 1918, all women over 21 in 1928. From 1948 a universal register was compiled annually.

Electoral registers are genealogically valuable because:

  • They run annually — unlike the decennial census
  • They give address by street and house number
  • They list all qualified voters at an address, potentially giving multiple male family members together
  • The absence of an expected name indicates departure, death, or disqualification

Electoral registers from 1832 to 1922 are held at county record offices and the British Library; post-1948 registers are also held by local councils and are available via commercial websites and some archives. The British Library holds a near-complete UK set. Ancestry holds many from the 20th century. Pre-1832, poll books recorded how each voter actually voted (by name) in contested elections — these run from the 17th century and are sometimes even richer than registers.

Rate books and valuation records

Every English parish levied local rates (a property tax) to fund the poor law, church repairs, and local maintenance. Rate books, listing every property and its rateable occupier, survive from the 18th century onward and are held at county record offices. They provide year-by-year address tracking between censuses — essentially an annual census substitute for property occupiers. Rate books are particularly useful for the period 1780–1841 before any national census coverage existed.

Guild records and apprenticeship registers

In urban and craft economies, guilds (livery companies in London, incorporated trades in Scottish burghs) controlled entry to skilled trades through an apprenticeship system. Apprenticeship records — often dating from the 17th century — give:

  • The apprentice's name, age, and often father's name and place of origin
  • The master's name, trade, and parish
  • The term of apprenticeship (usually 7 years)
  • The premium paid (cash sum to the master)

The most comprehensive English apprenticeship source is the IR1 series at TNA: apprenticeship duty records 1710–1811, indexed by both master and apprentice on Ancestry and FamilySearch. London's livery company records are held at the relevant companies and at Guildhall Library / London Metropolitan Archives — many are published or indexed. Scottish burgh records (held at local archives and NRS) often include burgess rolls listing freemen admitted to trade.

Occupational licensing and professional records

From the 19th century, many trades and professions required licensing, registration, or examination. Records of these requirements provide genealogically useful data:

  • Medical registers: from 1858, all qualified medical practitioners in Britain were required to register with the General Medical Council (GMC). The Medical Register is annual and gives the practitioner's name, address, qualifications, and medical school. Digitised historic editions exist.
  • Law Society rolls: solicitors admitted to the Law Society from 1844 are listed in annual Law Lists. Barristers are listed in annual Bar Directories.
  • Clergy registers: deacons and priests ordained in the Church of England appear in the Clergy List and Crockford's Clerical Directory (annual from 1858).
  • Schoolmaster licences: pre-1870, schoolmasters needed diocesan licences in many Anglican contexts; these are held in diocesan archives.
  • Customs and excise officers: HM Customs and Excise kept detailed staff records (CUST series at TNA) — officers appear by name, posting, and sometimes family details.

US occupational records

American occupational records equivalent to the UK guild system are less centralised but include:

  • Labor union records: trade union membership lists from the late 19th century; some are digitised or held at the Walter P. Reuther Library (Wayne State) or the Tamiment Library (NYU). A union membership card often gives birthplace and physical description.
  • Professional licensing records: state-level licensing for doctors (state medical boards), lawyers (state bar admission records), teachers (state board of education), and other professionals.
  • City and county employee records: police and fire department personnel files, courthouse employee records, and school board records — often held at city or county archives.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opens a slim printed volume — its cover reads 'Electoral Register, Manchester Parliamentary Borough, 1878.' The pages are columns of names and street addresses, hundreds per page.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The census is taken every ten years. What do you do with the nine years in between? For England, you have the electoral register: annual, listing every qualified voter by address, published by the county. Before 1918 only men with a property qualification voted — which excludes many working-class men — but from 1918 it covers every adult. A family in a Manchester street in 1881 to 1891 can be tracked year by year through the registers. You watch the sons appear as they reach voting age. You watch a name disappear when a man dies. It is almost a continuous record.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And before the Reform Act of 1832 — the poll books. When voting was open and public, the clerk recorded not just who was qualified to vote, but how they voted. Every contested election from the 17th century onward produced a poll book. Your ancestor's name, his qualification, his candidate. These are held at county record offices and the British Library. For the period before 1832, they are often the only annual record of an adult man's existence in a particular parish.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And the apprenticeship records — the IR1 series at the National Archives: apprenticeship duty records from 1710 to 1811, indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. A boy who was apprenticed to a cordwainer in 1755 appears in the index: his name, his father's name, his father's parish of origin, his master's name, and the premium paid. That father's name and parish can take you back a generation without a single church register.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Anchor non-census records

Retrieve from memory:

  • How often were British electoral registers compiled, and why does this make them useful between censuses?
  • What are poll books and from what period do they survive?
  • What information does an apprenticeship record (IR1) typically contain?
  • What is Crockford's Clerical Directory and what does it record?
  • Name one US equivalent occupational record type.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
British electoral registers were compiled annually, making them a year-by-year tracking tool between decennial censuses. They give address by street and house number, list all qualified voters at an address, and their absence in one year can indicate departure or death.

Poll books recorded how each qualified voter actually voted in contested elections, listed by name and qualification. They run from the 17th century to 1872 (when the Ballot Act introduced secret voting) and are held at county record offices and the British Library. Before the 1832 Reform Act, they are often the only annual record of an adult man's existence in a particular parish.

An IR1 apprenticeship record typically contains: the apprentice's name, age, and father's name and place of origin; the master's name, trade, and parish; the term of apprenticeship; and the premium paid. The father's details can take a researcher back a generation.

Crockford's Clerical Directory (annual from 1858) lists every ordained deacon and priest in the Church of England, giving name, qualifications, posting, and sometimes date of ordination — a comprehensive record of Anglican clergy throughout the later Victorian period.

US equivalent occupational records include: trade union membership records (held at labour libraries), state professional licensing records for doctors, lawyers, and teachers, and city/county employee personnel files.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
Tracking a family between censuses

Your ancestor James Walsh appears in the 1871 census at 15 Cork Street, Manchester, aged 35, as a tailor. He appears in the 1881 census at 42 Regent Road, Manchester, aged 45, still as a tailor. You want to understand when and why he moved address.

Design a research strategy (300–400 words) using the record types covered in this chunk to: (1) track James between 1871 and 1881; (2) investigate whether his occupation changed during this period; and (3) establish when, precisely, he moved from Cork Street to Regent Road.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
To track James Walsh between 1871 and 1881 and investigate his move and occupation:

1. Electoral registers (1872–1880): Manchester's annual electoral registers would list James Walsh by address each year if he qualified to vote (as a male property holder after 1867). Searching these registers at Manchester Central Library or on Ancestry's UK electoral register collection would show exactly which year his name shifts from 15 Cork Street to 42 Regent Road — potentially pinpointing the move to a single year.

2. Rate books: Manchester parish rate books for the relevant streets would confirm when James first appeared as the rated occupier of 42 Regent Road and when he ceased to be rated at 15 Cork Street. These are held at Manchester Archives and Local Studies. If the rate book records the occupier annually, the transition year should be identifiable.

3. Trade directories: Kelly's Directories for Manchester (and Slater's or Pigot's for earlier years) would list 'Walsh, James, tailor' by address and year. Directory entries were compiled in the preceding year, so a 1876 directory reflects James's address in 1875. Tracking his directory address year by year through the 1870s would confirm and refine the electoral register finding.

4. Occupational records: If James was a member of the Journeymen Tailors' trade union (active in Manchester in this period), union membership records might give his address at admission and whether his membership was continuous. Manchester archives may hold local union records.

5. Newspaper search: Manchester newspapers (British Newspaper Archive) sometimes carried items about craftsmen, court cases (debt or property disputes), or social notices that might explain a change of address — a business failure, a new workshop, or a family dispute.

Expected outcome: combining electoral registers and trade directories should narrow the move from a ten-year gap to a single year, and the rate books would confirm the transition precisely.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend what an electoral register is and why genealogists value it so highly when researching families in the years between census years.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Pre-1872 records of how each qualified voter voted in contested British elections — earlier than electoral registers and listing names by parish, held at county record offices and the British Library.
Annual parish records listing the rated occupier of every property, used to levy the poor rate; survive from the 18th century and provide year-by-year address tracking between censuses.
A TNA series covering English and Welsh apprenticeship indentures 1710–1811, indexed by master and apprentice; gives father's name and parish, making it a bridge between generations.
Annual directory of Church of England clergy from 1858, giving name, qualifications, and posting — the authoritative reference for tracing Anglican ordained ancestors.
The main repository for Greater London historical records, including livery company apprenticeship registers, parish records, and probate records from the City of London.

questions.questionHtml: What are British poll books and from what period do they typically survive?
options: Records of how each qualified voter voted in contested elections, surviving from the 17th century to 1872 when the Ballot Act introduced secret voting
Annual lists of everyone registered to vote in local council elections, from 1832
The weekly parish register of communicants, compiled by the incumbent
Government employment records for civil servants, from the 18th century
questions.correctAnswer: Records of how each qualified voter voted in contested elections, surviving from the 17th century to 1872 when the Ballot Act introduced secret voting
questions.explanationHtml: Poll books were produced for contested parliamentary elections from the 17th century until the Ballot Act 1872 introduced secret voting. Each entry names the voter, their qualification (e.g. freehold property, burgess right), and their candidate. Before the 1832 Reform Act, the franchise was highly restricted, meaning only a small proportion of adult men appear — but for those who do, the poll book is often the only annual record of their presence in a place.

questions.questionHtml: You find a man named Thomas Kelly in the 1841 and 1861 English censuses but cannot find him in 1851. Which of the following is the most productive next step?
options: Search the 1851 electoral register and local rate books for Thomas Kelly — if he was a qualified voter or property occupier, he would appear annually regardless of the census
Conclude he emigrated between 1841 and 1861 and search US passenger lists
The 1851 census is missing for his county — accept the gap as unresolvable
Search the 1871 census for him instead and work backwards
questions.correctAnswer: Search the 1851 electoral register and local rate books for Thomas Kelly — if he was a qualified voter or property occupier, he would appear annually regardless of the census
questions.explanationHtml: A missing census entry does not mean a family disappeared — it often means a transcription error, a temporary absence on census night, or a missed household. The electoral register and rate books run annually and are independent of the census. If Thomas appears in both in 1850 and 1852 at the same address, he was simply missed by the census enumerator or misindexed. The annual records confirm his continuous residence. Only if he is absent from the electoral register for the whole period would emigration or death become the working hypothesis.

questions.questionHtml: An apprenticeship record (IR1) for 1780 shows 'William Walsh, son of Thomas Walsh of Cork Street, Dublin, shoemaker, apprenticed to John Murphy, cordwainer, London.' What is the genealogical value of this entry beyond confirming William Walsh existed?
options: It gives Thomas Walsh's name, occupation (shoemaker), and place of residence (Cork Street, Dublin) — potentially identifying the father of the known ancestor William Walsh and providing a Dublin address to search in Irish records
The entry confirms William Walsh's religion, since all London apprentices were Anglican
It proves William Walsh emigrated from Ireland, which can be used to skip searching English records for his birth
It identifies the mother of William Walsh because all IR1 entries include both parents
questions.correctAnswer: It gives Thomas Walsh's name, occupation (shoemaker), and place of residence (Cork Street, Dublin) — potentially identifying the father of the known ancestor William Walsh and providing a Dublin address to search in Irish records
questions.explanationHtml: The IR1 apprenticeship entry names the father (or guardian), his occupation, and his place of residence — this is why the series is so genealogically valuable. The father's name and address can be taken back to Irish records: Dublin Catholic parish registers, Dublin city directories, and Dublin rate books can all now be searched for Thomas Walsh, shoemaker, Cork Street. This effectively bridges from the London-based apprentice to his Dublin origin without requiring any intermediate English vital record. The IR1 does not typically give the mother's name, and no inference about religion follows from being apprenticed in London.
